extracted.intended_audience: mathematics educators, mathematics education researchers, mathematicians, and mathematics students
extracted.subtask_description: A conceptual framework for the values and norms that define acceptable mathematical proofs and the implications for teaching, learning, and researching proof practice. Useful for evaluating proofs (professional and student) and guiding pedagogical choices about rigor and presentation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Establishing a priori truth
rubrics_metrics.description: Proofs adhere to the value of establishing a priori truth.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: From the abstract: one of the central mathematical values is that proofs establish a priori truth. This is presented as a core value that proofs aim to realize, against which norms (acceptable reasoning, rigor, etc.) are judged.

rubrics_metrics.name: Employing decontextualized reasoning
rubrics_metrics.description: Proofs employ decontextualized reasoning as a value of mathematical proof practice.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The paper lists 'employing decontextualized reasoning' as a value — i.e., reasoning that is not tied to particular empirical contexts. This informs expectations that proofs generalize beyond specific examples or situations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Increasing mathematical understanding
rubrics_metrics.description: Proofs should increase mathematical understanding (a pedagogical and epistemic value).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The authors explicitly include 'increasing mathematical understanding' among the values. They note pedagogical implications: mathematicians sometimes relax formal rigor in lectures to increase students' understanding (Lai & Weber, 2014). Thus evaluation may trade off formal strictness for explanatory power in pedagogical contexts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Maintaining consistent standards for acceptable reasoning across domains
rubrics_metrics.description: Proof practice should maintain consistent standards for acceptable reasoning across mathematical domains.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: From the abstract: maintaining consistent standards is given as a value. The paper argues that community norms express and uphold such consistency, although subgroups (e.g., experimental mathematicians) may systematically deviate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Correctness relative to a reference theory (axioms, definitions, rules of inference)
rubrics_metrics.description: The correctness of a proof is necessarily dependent upon the axioms, definitions, and rules of inference within the reference theory.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: As noted (Mariotti, 2006), whether a proof is 'correct' depends on the background formal/semantic framework — proofs are evaluated with respect to the chosen axioms, definitions, and inference rules. This is a procedural/technical standard for assessing formal validity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Standards of rigor used in evaluation
rubrics_metrics.description: Rigor is a norm employed when evaluating proofs, though its application may vary by context and audience.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The paper observes that mathematicians use stricter standards of rigor when assessing student proofs than they do when presenting proofs in lectures or textbooks (they may omit detail to enhance understanding). Evaluators should therefore consider both the intended audience and context when judging a proof's adequacy (Lew, 2016; Lai & Weber, 2014).

rubrics_metrics.name: Students' acceptance of mathematical values as part of apprenticeship
rubrics_metrics.description: Students' acceptance of the community's mathematical values is integral to their apprenticeship into proof practice.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: From the abstract: if students do not perceive or accept the values (e.g., a priori truth, decontextualization, standards of rigor), they will likely have difficulty adhering to the norms that uphold them and will find proof confusing. This is a sociocognitive criterion for successful learning.

rubrics_metrics.name: Contextual appropriateness of proofs (lecture vs textbook vs student-generated)
rubrics_metrics.description: Expectations for what counts as an acceptable proof depend on context (lecture, textbook, student-generated, etc.).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Lew (2016) and other discussion indicate that different contexts have different conventions; students often fail to account for these differences. Evaluators and instructors should make context-specific norms explicit when judging proofs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tolerance for error and correction practices
rubrics_metrics.description: Community tolerance for error in mathematical practice and publication influences norms about acceptable proofs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The authors cite Fallis (2002) and Grcar (2013) discussing whether mathematics has lower tolerance for error than other sciences. Consideration of error tolerance (and mechanisms for correction) affects judgments about acceptability and the role of probabilistic/experimental evidence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Permitted methodological deviations (e.g., experimental mathematics)
rubrics_metrics.description: Subgroups (such as experimental mathematicians) may reject or systematically breach certain canonical values/norms, but their practices are recognized as distinct within the community.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The paper notes that experimental mathematicians sometimes reject values like strict deductive emphasis; their classification and philosophical defense of such breaches imply that community norms can accommodate disciplined methodological variation. Evaluators should recognize when a departure is a community-accepted sub-practice versus a norm violation.
